# Voltage Stability in Automotive Cigarette Lighter Sockets

Running a Mini-ITX PC off a vehicle's auxiliary power outlet introduces a specific set of electrical challenges that differ significantly from desktop setups. The core concern isn't just whether the car provides 12V; it is understanding how much that voltage fluctuates under load and during engine events, specifically when evaluating devices like the picoPSU-80.

Automotive electrical systems are not regulated power plants in the way a wall outlet or an ATX PSU is. They are essentially unregulated sources tied directly to the alternator output once the engine spins. While a car battery sits at roughly 12.6V when the vehicle is off and resting, this number shifts dramatically under operation. A standard lead-acid battery can sag significantly if you attempt to draw high current without the alternator compensating, but in most vehicles, the alternator actively maintains system voltage between 13.5V and 14.8V while running.

The documentation for the picoPSU-80 explicitly states an over-voltage shutdown threshold of approximately 13–13.5V. This is a critical specification because it defines your operational window. If your car's voltage regulation pushes above this limit, the power supply will cut power to protect itself. Conversely, the unit requires a minimum input current capability (it draws from the source) and typically needs the input voltage to stay within a functional range, often cited by community consensus as ±10% of nominal 12V.

This ±10% tolerance translates to an acceptable input range of roughly 10.8V to 13.2V. Here lies the primary risk: starting conditions. When you first turn on your car's ignition, the alternator may not be fully engaged or regulated yet. Furthermore, if multiple accessories (lights, radio, climate control) are drawing current simultaneously while your PC turns on, the voltage can dip below 10.8V momentarily. The picoPSU-80 will fail to start or reset in this scenario because it cannot regulate output without a stable input rail above its minimum threshold.

For a system consuming around 30W (which draws roughly 2.5A at 12V), the load is manageable for modern alternators, but the transient response of cheap wiring can still cause dips. If you route your power through long gauge wires or shared circuits with high-drain devices like headlights, voltage drop becomes a real factor. Even if the source is "dedicated," poor grounding or undersized cables can mimic a weak supply.

The M3-ATX DC-DC converter offers a compelling alternative by accepting 6–24V input and providing an isolated, regulated output. This device essentially decouples your PC from the car's electrical noise and voltage swings. It handles the wide swing between a resting battery (12.6V) and alternator charging (14.5V) internally, ensuring the Mini-ITX board always sees a pristine 12V regardless of engine state.

However, cost is a valid constraint for many embedded projects. If you proceed with the $25 picoPSU-80, you must implement strict logic to prevent startup issues. You can add a simple P-channel MOSFET or a relay controlled by an Arduino or ESP32 that monitors the bus voltage. The microcontroller checks if voltage is stable above 12V before enabling the power rail to the PC. This prevents the picoPSU from cycling on and off during engine cranking or low-voltage transients.

Alternatively, you can physically disconnect the input of the picoPSU with a heavy-duty switch that only engages after the car's voltage has been confirmed stable for several seconds post-ignition. While this adds complexity to your harness, it is far cheaper than upgrading the power supply unit itself. Remember that cheap DC-DC converters are not immune to noise; ensure you have adequate decoupling capacitors near the picoPSU input and output pins to filter out ignition spikes and radio frequency interference common in cabin environments.

If your application demands absolute reliability without custom firmware or hardware logic, the M3-ATX is the safer investment. It removes the voltage monitoring burden from your software stack entirely, allowing you to focus on the embedded code rather than debugging brownouts caused by a car's electrical quirks.
